'''Rabia Salihu Sa'id'''{{Pronunciation|Ha-Rabia Salihu Sa'id.ogg|help=no}}{{efn|Her surname is also spelled Said,<ref name="World Academy" /> Sai'id,<ref name=SNS>{{cite news | url=https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-401630063.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170922050525/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-401630063.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 22, 2017 | title=Early-Career Women Scientists from Developing Countries Honored at Aaas Annual Meeting|work=State News Service|via=HighBeam Research|date= February 14, 2015| url-access=subscription |access-date=December 14, 2016}}</ref> and Saeed.<ref name=Covenant />}} (born on 21 April 1963) is a Nigerian [[physicist]], professor of atmospheric and space-weather physics, and a researcher at [[Bayero University Kano]].  She conducts research in [[Atmospheric physics|atmospheric]] and [[space weather|space weather physics]], [[particle physics]], and electronics. Sa'id is an advocate and mentor for young women in science with the Visiola Foundation and [[Peace Corps]]; she co-founded Nigeria's Association of Women Physicists. She is an advocate and mentor of Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education and is a facilitator for the [[British Council]]'s Active Citizens' Programme.{{Citation needed|date=August 2022}}

Sai'd has received fellowships from Institute of Applied Physics in [[Bern, Switzerland]] and the [[Ford Foundation]] and made a fellow of African Scientific Institute (ASI). In 2015, she received an Elsevier Foundation Award for Women Scientists in the Developing World.<ref name=AAAS>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aaas.org/news/early-career-women-scientists-developing-countries-honored-aaas-annual-meeting|title=Early-Career Women Scientists From Developing Countries Honored at AAAS Annual Meeting|date=10 February 2015|newspaper=AAAS - The World's Largest General Scientific Society|access-date=10 December 2016 }}</ref> She was also recognised in 2015 by the [[British Council]] for her community work, and by the [[BBC]] as part of their ''[[100 Women (BBC)|100 Women]]'' series.{{Citation needed|date=August 2022}}

==Personal life==
Rabia Sa'id was born in the year 1963 in Wangara, a town in [[Gezawa]] local government area of [[Kano State]], Northern [[Nigeria]],<ref name="BUK">{{cite news|url=https://buk.academia.edu/RABIASALIHUSAID|title=Rabia Salihu Sa'id|website=Bayero University|access-date=1 December 2016}}</ref> where girls have few education opportunities, many marry in their teens, and women are expected to stay at home.<ref name="Nature Developing world" />{{efn|According to the [[Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]], Nigeria ranks very low in its treatment of women. The government, though, is working to improve opportunities for women.<ref name="Nature Developing world" />}} Her father, however, wanted her to become a doctor. He was an officer in the Nigerian Army<ref name="Nature Developing world" /> who had two wives and fathered ten children.<ref name="Bert" />

Sa'id attended an Army school at the top of her class.<ref name="Bert" /> She chose to marry at the age of 18, once she graduated from a secondary school.<ref name="Nature Developing world" /><ref name=SNS /> She is a mother of six.<ref name="NPR">{{cite web|last1=Venton|first1=Danielle|title=Tough As Nails: Female Scientists Rise Up In Nigeria|date=17 February 2015|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2015/02/17/386549295/tough-as-nails-women-scientists-rise-up-in-nigeria|website=NPR|access-date=14 December 2016}}</ref> Two of her children needed medical care (one of them was born with [[club foot]] and another with [[Sickle-cell disease|sickle-cell anemia]]), which added to her personal challenge to obtain higher education degrees.<ref name="Nature Developing world">{{Cite journal|last=Moskvitch|first=Katia|date=5 March 2015|title=Developing world: The minority minority|journal=Nature|volume=519|issue=7541|pages=20–23|doi=10.1038/519020a|pmid=25739613|bibcode=2015Natur.519...20M|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Career==

===Education and early career===
Sa'id began her university education at the age of 29 and ran a nursery school to pay for her education.<ref name="Nature Developing world" /> She holds Bachelor of Science, Masters of Science and Ph.D degrees in [[Physics]] from [[Bayero University Kano]].<ref name="Schemm" />{{efn|UNESCO finds that about 24% of doctoral students in the science fields are women. In 2013, Sa'id co-authored a report that found that 5–20% of Nigerian university students enrolled in physics were women.<ref name="Nature Developing world" /> Women are about 14% of the Nigerian academics.<ref name="NPR" />}}  In September 1999, she commenced work as a Graduate Assistant at Bayero University.<ref name="BBC">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p0306cj9|title=Nigerian Physicist sold her Jewellery for Science|work=Discovery|publisher=[[BBC World Service]]|author=Claudia Hammond|access-date=1 December 2016|author-link=Claudia Hammond}}</ref> In 2002, on the International Fellowships Program (IFP) of the [[Ford Foundation]], she studied for an M.Sc degree in Environment and Development from the [[University of Reading]], United Kingdom.<ref name="FF">{{cite web|title=Getting Ahead Through Higher Education - Ford Foundation Fellowships - 2003-11-07|publisher=Voice of America|orig-year=2003|date=30 October 2009|url=https://www.voanews.com/a/a-13-a-2003-11-07-44-getting/297631.html|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref><ref name="NA Ten Distinguished" />

===Educator===
She began working in 1999 for the Bayero University<ref name="BBC" /> and is now a professor of undergraduate and graduate level courses in atmospheric and space-weather physics.<ref name="Nature Developing world" /><ref name="Schemm" />{{efn|In April 2012, militants of the Islamist group [[Boko Haram]] killed 16 people and wounded many more at a church on the university campus, as part of a campaign to eliminate Western education and establish an Islamic State. Sa'id knew two of the people who died that day; She was home with her children. Security has been built up at the university since the attack.<ref name="Nature Developing world" />}} By 2015, she was Deputy Dean at the Student Affairs Division of the university.<ref name=AAAS />

===Research===
She received a research post at the university,<ref name="Nature Developing world" /> where she conducts research in [[Atmospheric physics|atmospheric]] and [[space weather|space weather physics]], [[particle physics]], and electronics. Her research is conducted to solve Nigerian environmental challenges.<ref name="Schemm"/> To reduce the number of trees cut down for firewood, for instance, one of her study was about use scraps of wood from carpentry projects for briquettes that could be used as a fuel, thereby reducing the rate at which the country's forests are diminished. She also gathers atmospheric data<ref name="Schemm"/> and studies the effects of [[deforestation]]<ref name="NPR" /> and [[mineral dust|dust aerosols]] on climate temperatures.<ref name="Nature Developing world" /> Her goal is to encourage greater reliance in Nigeria on renewable energy sources—like wind power, solar energy, and hydropower—that are less harmful to the environment than [[fossil fuel]]s.<ref name="FF" /><ref name="Bert" />

In 2010, she worked with Dr. C. Matzler, a scientist in terrestrial and atmospheric remote sensing, at the Institute of Applied Physics, University of Bern, Switzerland as a visiting research scientist for four months.<ref name="NA Ten Distinguished" /> In January 2013, she was made an African Scientific Institute (ASI) Fellow in Physics,<ref>{{cite web | url=http://asi-org.net/fellows-in-physics/ | title=Fellows in Physics | website=African Scientific Institute | access-date=14 December 2016 | archive-date=4 August 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804173530/http://asi-org.net/fellows-in-physics/ | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.ligali.org/newsletter/nyansapo_07feb13.htm | title=African Scientific Institute|date=7 February 2013|website=Legali|access-date=14 December 2016}}</ref> which is an honorary association and [[think tank]] of academics, researchers, and business people.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://asi-org.net/asi-fellows/ | title=ASI Fellows |access-date=14 December 2016}}</ref>

===STEM outreach===
Sa'id is active in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics]] (STEM) outreach.<ref name="AA girls" />  She is a co-founder of Nigeria's Association of Women Physicists in 2011, which encourages women to become physicists, seeks to improve physics education in schools, and gives prizes to young women.<ref name="Nature Developing world" /> Sa'id also encourages participation of young people by mentoring them in local and national science projects,<ref name="Schemm"/> volunteering for the Peace Corps Nigeria Alumni Foundation and Visiola Foundation.<ref name="NA Ten Distinguished" />{{efn|As part of her [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] outreach work, Sa'id gave the [[keynote address]] at the Annual Gala Dinner of the Visiola Foundation on 2 May 2015 in [[Abuja]].<ref>{{cite web|title=The Visiola Foundation Launches its '1,000 Female African STEM Pros' Campaign|publisher=The Visiola Foundation|date=15 May 2015|url=http://www.visiolafoundation.org/news/the-visiola-foundation-launches-its-1000-female-african-stem-pros-campaign/|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref>}} According to Rabia Salihu, she is active in STEM outreach because there is group pressure and obstacles that girls, particularly those in northern Nigeria, must overcome to pursue degrees and careers in these fields. In addition, "more girls in science will mean that the solutions that science provides are not just tailored to the needs of a single gender."<ref name="AA girls">{{cite news | url=http://allafrica.com/stories/201510080424.html | title=Nigeria: Girls Urged to Develop Confidence in Maths, Science | newspaper=Daily Trust (Abuja) |first=Chidimma C. |last=Okeke | via=AllAfrica |date=7 October 2015 |access-date=14 December 2016}}</ref>{{efn|She tells women in northern Nigeria about how she pursued university degrees while a young mother, 10 years out of secondary school, to encourage them to go to college.<ref name=SNS />}} In addition, there is greater appreciation for careers where there are practical applications, like banking and medicine.<ref name=Covenant>{{cite web | url=http://covenantuniversity.edu.ng/layout/set/print/News/Covenant-University-Hosts-2nd-National-Conference-of-Women-in-Physics | title=Covenant University Hosts 2nd National Conference of Women in Physics | website=Covenant University | date=17 June 2013 | access-date=14 December 2016 | archive-date=20 December 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220132117/http://covenantuniversity.edu.ng/layout/set/print/News/Covenant-University-Hosts-2nd-National-Conference-of-Women-in-Physics | url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Recognition===
In 2015 she was a recipient of one of the five Elsevier Foundation Awards for Women Scientists in the Developing World.<ref name="Bert">{{cite web|last=Bert|first=Alison|title=5 women scientists tell their stories of hard-earned success|website=Elsevier Connect
|publisher=Elsevier|date=23 February 2015|url=https://www.elsevier.com/connect/5-women-scientists-tell-their-stories-of-hard-earned-success|access-date=11 December 2016}}</ref> Presented in partnership with the [[Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World]] (OWSD) and [[The World Academy of Sciences]] (TWAS), the awards that year were for the physics and mathematics fields, with Sa'id's award in the field of [[atmospheric physics]].<ref name="Schemm">{{cite web|last=Schemm|first=Ylann|title=Here are the winners of the Women in Science Elsevier Foundation Awards|date=10 February 2015|website=Elsevier Connect|publisher=Elsevier|url=https://www.elsevier.com/connect/women-in-physics-and-math-to-receive-elsevier-foundation-awards-at-aaas-meeting|access-date=11 December 2016}}</ref> She received the award for her work on Nigerian environmental challenges,<ref name="Bert" /> which was presented on 14 February 2015 at the Annual Meeting of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) in San Jose, California.<ref name="World Academy" />{{efn|The award included a prize of [[USD|$]]5000 and free attendance at a workshop or conference at the [[Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] (ICTP).<ref name="Schemm"/><ref name="World Academy">{{cite journal|title=Today's scholars, tomorrow's leaders|publisher=The World Academy of Sciences|url=http://twas.org/sites/default/files/nl26-4_p20-21-elsevier.pdf|access-date=11 December 2016|volume=26|number=4|year=2014|pages=20–21|archive-date=30 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160730023207/http://twas.org/sites/default/files/nl26-4_p20-21-elsevier.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>}}

In August 2015, Sa'id was interviewed by BBC journalist [[Claudia Hammond]] for a feature on the [[BBC World Service]],<ref name="BBC"/> and was featured in the [[BBC]]'s annual ''[[100 Women (BBC)|100 Women]]'' series, highlighting her efforts to promote science education in Nigeria.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/special/2015/newsspec_12497/content/english/index.html?v=0.1.21&hostid=www.bbc.com&hostUrl=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.bbc.com%2Fnews%2Fworld-34745739&iframeUID=responsive-iframe-58024518&onbbcdomain=true#facewall_78|title=Who are the 100 women?|work=[[BBC]]|access-date=1 December 2016}}</ref> The following year (2016) she was featured in online magazine ''The Nigerian Academia'' in a list of distinguished Nigerian women in science.<ref name="NA Ten Distinguished">{{cite news|newspaper=The Nigerian Academia|title=Ten Distinguished Nigerian Women In Science|date=21 October 2016|url=http://www.thenigerianacademia.com/2016/10/21/ten-distinguished-nigerian-women-in-science/|access-date=12 December 2016|archive-date=17 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181217221810/http://www.thenigerianacademia.com/2016/10/21/ten-distinguished-nigerian-women-in-science/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Advocate==
In addition to the mentoring that she does for the Peace Corps and Visiola for STEM outreach, she is a facilitator for the [[British Council]] Active Citizens' Programme, who encourages young people to develop efficient and peaceful communication skills for sustainable development in their communities.<ref name="NA Ten Distinguished" />

She was one of nine people honored as "women advocates and champions" in Nigeria in March 2015 as part of [[International Women's Day]] by the British Council and two of its development programmes, the Nigeria Stability and Reconciliation Programme (NSRP) and the Justice for All (J4A) programme.<ref>{{cite web|title=International Women's Day: British Council To Honour Nine Women|publisher=International Centre for Investigative Reporting|date=7 March 2015|url=http://icirnigeria.org/international-womens-day-british-council-to-honour-nine-women/|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref>{{efn|Champions are "those who have distinguished themselves in works related to peacebuilding, women’s participation in public service and decision making and women in creative enterprise." They are profiled in workshops, radio talk shows, social media, and round table discussions, such as events at Bayero University Kano with its students to discuss women champions and their role in peace building, enterprise, or academia.<ref>{{Cite news | url=http://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/more-news/177716-british-council-set-to-mark-womens-day.html | title=British Council set to mark women's day|date=1 March 2015|newspaper=[[Premium Times]]|location=Nigeria |access-date=14 December 2016}}</ref>}}
